final_proof:
**Conventions.** $M$ locally Euclidean of dimension $d$: every point of $M$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ with a homeomorphism $\phi : V \to W$ onto an open subset $W \subseteq \R^d$. (If the definition only asks for a neighbourhood $N$ of $m$ homeomorphic to an open $W\subseteq\R^d$ via $\phi$, replace $N$ by $V=\operatorname{int}N \ni m$: $V$ is open in $N$, so $\phi(V)$ is open in $W$, hence open in $\R^d$, and $\phi|_V : V\to\phi(V)$ is a homeomorphism.) A local basis of $m$ is a family $\mathcal B$ of open sets containing $m$ such that every open set $O \ni m$ contains some member of $\mathcal B$. $B(x,s)=\{y\in\R^d : \|y-x\|<s\}$.

**Proof.** Fix $m\in M$ and $V$, $\phi : V\to W$ as above; let $x=\phi(m)\in W$. Since $W$ is open in $\R^d$, choose $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq W$. For $n\in\N$ put $r_n = r/(n+1)$ and
$$U_n = \phi^{-1}\big(B(x,r_n)\big).$$

*(1) Each $U_n$ is an open set containing $m$.* $B(x,r_n)\subseteq B(x,r)\subseteq W$ is open in $\R^d$, hence open in $W$. By continuity of $\phi$, $U_n$ is open in $V$; as $V$ is open in $M$, $U_n$ is open in $M$. Also $\phi(m)=x\in B(x,r_n)$, so $m\in U_n$.

*(2) Each $U_n$ is a homeomorphic image of an open ball of $\R^d$.* $\psi=\phi^{-1}:W\to V$ is a homeomorphism; its restriction to the subset $B(x,r_n)\subseteq W$ is a continuous bijection $B(x,r_n)\to\psi(B(x,r_n))=U_n$ whose inverse is the restriction $\phi|_{U_n}$, also continuous (restrictions of continuous maps to subspaces are continuous, with codomains restricted to the images). Hence $U_n$ is the image of the open ball $B(x,r_n)$ under the homeomorphism $\psi|_{B(x,r_n)}$.

*(3) $\{U_n\}_{n\in\N}$ is a local basis of $m$.* Let $O\subseteq M$ be open with $m\in O$. Then $O\cap V$ is open in $V$, so $\phi(O\cap V)$ is open in $W$ ($\phi$ is a homeomorphism, hence an open map onto $W$), and since $W$ is open in $\R^d$, $\phi(O\cap V)$ is open in $\R^d$. It contains $x=\phi(m)$, so there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq\phi(O\cap V)$. Choose $n\in\N$ with $r/(n+1)<\varepsilon$ (Archimedean property). Then $B(x,r_n)\subseteq B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq \phi(O\cap V)$, and applying $\phi^{-1}$ (a bijection $W\to V$),
$$U_n=\phi^{-1}(B(x,r_n))\subseteq \phi^{-1}(\phi(O\cap V)) = O\cap V\subseteq O.$$

The family is indexed by $\N$, hence countable. (If local bases are allowed to consist of arbitrary neighbourhoods, the same family works: every neighbourhood of $m$ contains an open set $O\ni m$, which contains some $U_n$.) The case $d=0$ is included: then $\R^0=\{0\}$ and every open ball is $\{0\}$, and all steps above hold verbatim. $\blacksquare$
